common_name: Ruby Glow Witch Hazel (Copper-Red Midseason Winter Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Ruby Glow' opens its flowers in midwinter, later than 'Arnold Promise' but overlapping with 'Diane' and 'Jelena', extending the witch hazel bloom season when planted alongside earlier and later cultivars.

directions: Ruby Glow is an older hybrid witch hazel selection valued for its deep coppery red-orange flowers, a shade between the garnet red of 'Diane' and the burnt orange of 'Jelena', carried in dense clusters on bare branches in the coldest weeks of the year. It grows into an upright, vase-shaped, multi-stemmed shrub that is somewhat more restrained in size than the largest intermedia cultivars, making it useful where a smaller winter accent shrub is needed near a path or window. Fall foliage turns respectable shades of orange and yellow before dropping to reveal the flower buds already formed for the following winter. Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun and prune only lightly right after flowering, since witch hazel blooms on old wood.

common_name: Westerstede Witch Hazel (Early Pale Yellow Winter Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Westerstede' is among the earliest intermedia witch hazels to open, so site it where its pale winter flowers are visible from indoors before most other bloom begins.

directions: Bred in Germany, Westerstede is prized as one of the earliest-flowering hybrid witch hazels, opening pale, soft sulfur-yellow, spidery flowers in the depths of winter ahead of most other intermedia cultivars, and holding them well through cold snaps. The narrow, ribbon-like petals are carried in dense clusters along upright, vase-shaped branches, giving a lighter, more airy winter display than the darker-colored cultivars. Good clear yellow fall foliage color follows the summer growing season before the shrub drops its leaves and repeats its early winter show. Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, and give it room to develop its naturally upright, spreading form without frequent pruning.

common_name: Brevipetala Chinese Witch Hazel (Deep Gold Very Fragrant Selection)

planting.note: Plant container or balled stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Brevipetala' is an old, long-cultivated Chinese witch hazel selection noted for unusually short, twisted petals and outstanding fragrance.

directions: Brevipetala is one of the oldest named selections of Chinese witch hazel, distinguished from the species by shorter, broader, twisted deep-gold petals emerging from a reddish-bronze calyx, giving the flowers a denser, more compact look than the finer strap-petaled species form. Its fragrance is exceptionally strong and sweet even by witch hazel standards, carrying readily on still winter air. The broad, rounded leaves turn soft yellow in fall on a multi-stemmed, vase-shaped shrub that eventually becomes quite substantial with age. Grow in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, sheltered from harsh winter wind, and prune only to remove damaged or crossing wood right after flowering.

common_name: Hidcote St. John's Wort (Large-Flowered Semi-Evergreen Garden Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Hidcote' does not come true from seed and is propagated by cuttings, prized for the largest flowers of any commonly grown garden Hypericum.

directions: Hidcote, named for the celebrated English Arts and Crafts garden where it was popularized, is one of the most widely planted ornamental St. John's worts, valued for exceptionally large, saucer-shaped, golden-yellow flowers up to three inches across with a prominent central boss of stamens, produced in a long, heavy flush from midsummer into early fall. The semi-evergreen, blue-green foliage holds on the mounded, rounded shrub through mild winters, dropping only in colder parts of its range. It tolerates a wide range of soils, including poor or chalky ground, and shrugs off summer heat and light drought once established, needing only an occasional hard prune in early spring to keep the mound dense and floriferous. Give it full sun for the heaviest bloom, though it tolerates and often benefits from part-day shade in hot summer climates.

common_name: Sunburst St. John's Wort (Compact Golden St. John's Wort Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Sunburst' is a compact, more floriferous selection of golden St. John's wort propagated by cuttings, tolerant of rocky or poor soils once established.

directions: Sunburst is a selected form of the native golden St. John's wort, chosen for a denser, more rounded habit and heavier bloom than seed-grown plants of the species, covering itself in large, bright golden-yellow flowers with showy brush-like stamens for several weeks in summer. The fine-textured, blue-green foliage and exfoliating bark give it appeal even out of bloom, and the persistent reddish seed capsules add subtle winter interest. Like the species, it is exceptionally drought and heat tolerant once established and thrives in dry, rocky, or shallow soils where many flowering shrubs struggle, making it a reliable choice for a sunny to lightly shaded border or naturalistic planting. Avoid consistently wet or poorly drained sites, which it does not tolerate as well as some other native Hypericum species.

common_name: Cobalt-n-Gold Kalm's St. John's Wort (Compact Blue-Foliage Native Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average to sandy, well-drained to seasonally wet soil in full sun; 'Cobalt-n-Gold' is a Proven Winners ColorChoice introduction selected for a tighter, more compact rounded habit than the species.

directions: Cobalt-n-Gold is a compact selection of the Great Lakes native Kalm's St. John's wort, bred for a tighter, more uniformly rounded mound than the straight species while keeping the same striking blue-green foliage and bright golden flowers with their prominent burst of stamens through summer. Its smaller stature suits foundation plantings, low hedges, and mixed borders where the species can eventually grow too large. Like the species it develops attractive exfoliating bark on older stems and tolerates both dry, sandy soil and periodically wet sites, plus wind and light salt exposure, making it useful along rain gardens and pond edges. A light shearing in early spring keeps the mound dense and encourages abundant new flowering wood.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade; Farges' clethra is a Chinese relative of Japanese clethra (C. barbinervis) grown for its exfoliating bark and midsummer flower racemes. Propagate from softwood cuttings in summer.

directions: Farges' clethra is a large, multi-stemmed deciduous shrub or small tree from the mountain forests of central China, closely related to the better-known Japanese clethra but somewhat less commonly grown outside specialist and botanic garden collections. Older stems develop attractively flaking, patchwork bark that adds interest to the winter garden, while long, upright to slightly arching racemes of small, fragrant white flowers open in mid- to late summer and draw bees in numbers. Clean, dark green foliage takes on yellow to bronze tones in fall before dropping. Site it in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade as a woodland-edge specimen or large shrub border accent where its bark and summer bloom can be appreciated up close.
